abstract: We present Piccolo, a family of multimodal decision models (0.8B to 27B) that coevolves model capabilities and training data via Agentic Data Engineering and recursive self-improvement (RSI). The models predict probabilities over candidate answers for general-purpose text and visual judgments, agent harnesses, data workflows, and interactive games. Piccolo-27B tops the Decision Index Vision Full leaderboard with a score of 75.59, while Piccolo-9B and Piccolo-4B achieve 68.35 and 67.46, respectively. All three rank first on the Private benchmark in their respective model-size categories. Research agents analyze model behavior, construct training data, conduct experiments, and use the results to refine subsequent proposals. Semantic slices and a shared research memory connect these actions across the model family's development. With training recipes comprising hundreds of thousands of examples, data selection and feedback-driven refinement are central to the self-improvement process. Our large-scale RSI exploration yields three counter-intuitive insights for decision-model development: (1) Backbone-recipe co-adaptation outweighs raw model recency: earlier backbones can surpass newer generations on visual tasks under identical recipes; (2) Targeted data curation enables 4B-9B models to rival 27B baselines on specialized workflows; and (3) Continuous loss reduction can decouple from and even degrade discrete decision accuracy. Together with the released weights and tools from the Data-Juicer and AgentScope ecosystems, Piccolo provides an actionable blueprint for building frontier decision models and scaling data-driven RSI.
title: Piccolo: Co-Evolving Decision Models and Data through Recursive Self-Improvement

abstract: Pre-trained models can read screens and reason about games, yet on an unfamiliar game, an agent still has to learn to play. We ask how an agent can self-improve on such a game from a few of its own attempts, in real-time visual games where the agent sees only the screen and the game keeps running while the agent thinks. We study two kinds of policy that can carry this improvement. In model as policy, a model selects actions during play; we adapt real-time chunking so that committed actions keep executing while the model reasons, and train a 2B controller for this interface. In code as policy, a model writes, tests, and revises a program between attempts, and the program acts during play. Across 170 GameWorld tasks, with at most eight one-minute executions per run, code as policy reaches 47.80% mean progress, against 30.90% for our trained controller, and leads in all five game categories. Improving the controller's weights on a single game, by contrast, yields only modest gains. These results favor letting a model think offline and storing what it learns in a program that acts in real time. Project repository: https://github.com/TabibitoQZP/SIGame
title: Think Offline, Act in Real Time: Self-Improving Visual Game Agents through Code

abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) is moving from the harness of prompts and tools around a base model toward the model itself. However, existing RSI still faces key challenges, including harness-bound gains that stay outside the base model, black-box supervision that reads only the model's outputs, and imprecise edits whose site and strength are fixed in advance. To address these challenges, we propose BaseRSI, a new paradigm of Recursive Harness Internalization: the base model improves its harness, then writes what the harness adds into its own weights through training-free edits, round after round on its own responses. To support this paradigm, we introduce ReGap, a mechanism that supervises every transformer block with the high-dimensional activation difference that the harness makes at that block alone, and updates the block's weights along this signal in a low-dimensional subspace. Building on this mechanism, we further propose ReKey, an algorithm that writes this signal by regression into a few key-value neurons of every block, and measures the site and strength of each edit on the model's own responses. Moreover, the base model fills every role of this recursion with forward passes alone, and its edits, written at different sites, compose in one checkpoint without refitting. Experimental results on ten visual reasoning benchmarks show that BaseRSI consistently improves a base vision-language model both in distribution and on held-out benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/beita6969/BaseRSI.
title: BaseRSI: Recursive Self-Improvement of a Base Vision-Language Model via Training-Free Harness Internalization

abstract: Improving the efficiency of training and inference infrastructure is a practical component of recursive self-improvement. Existing benchmarks for agent-driven optimization largely focus on individual software layers such as kernel, leaving unclear whether agents can deliver end-to-end performance gains under production workloads. We introduce RSIBench-Infra, a benchmark of 20 training and inference tasks spanning diverse model families and modalities, with deployments of up to 32 accelerators on NVIDIA GPUs and Ascend NPUs. Agents start from runnable baselines derived from official recipes and can modify the software stack across engine, kernel, and instruction levels. An OCI image-layer submission protocol captures these changes for reproducible deployment, while independent evaluation measures end-to-end performance under task-specific quality constraints. Across all task results, 66.2% exceed $1.10\times$ validated speedup. These results demonstrate that current agents can improve production-scale training and inference performance, but identifying effective optimization strategies and consistently translating local improvements into end-to-end gains remain challenging.
title: RSIBench-Infra: Can Agents Optimize Their Own Training and Inference Infrastructure at Production Scale?

abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to follow natural-language instructions, yet still fail frequently in closed-loop flight. Correcting these failures requires repairs, i.e., actions that avoid them at the states the policy itself reaches, which human pilots cannot label at scale and rule-based planners cannot supply reliably. In this paper, we present AeroRSI, a recursive self-improvement framework in which an aerial navigation policy iteratively learns from its own failures. Our key insight is that a failing policy should judge its own repairs by flying on from them. Judged in this way, its sampled actions and even rule-based proposals that hurt it when imitated directly become reliable supervision. Moreover, an episode terminates at its first failure, concealing subsequent failures until the earlier ones are repaired. AeroRSI thus renews its supervision in every round, anchoring the failures of the current policy, verifying repairs by its continuation, and distilling them while keeping its behavior elsewhere. On TravelUAV, three rounds raise the success rate of a supervised 2B-parameter policy from 46.4% to 67.5% and reduce collisions by half, surpassing the previous state of the art by 10.6 points from the same initialization without extra human labels or inference cost. Code and models are available at https://github.com/starsholic/AeroRSI.
title: AeroRSI: Recursive Self-Improvement for Aerial Vision-Language Navigation

abstract: Video evaluators play an important role in video generation, yet they miss motion defects, limiting the quality of generated videos. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) has made strong progress in mathematics and coding, where explicit verifiers provide reliable feedback on a single goal. Video evaluation poses two difficulties for RSI: it has no verifier, and it must judge many dimensions at once, such as physics, smoothness and dynamics, where a gain on one can cost another. We introduce EVA-RSI, a multi-agent framework for exploring RSI under these two constraints. We build a fixed proxy exam with construction-defined targets by applying controlled changes to videos, such as temporal reversal and frame dropping. These edits supply supervision without human annotation. A small set of human-labeled real videos anchors the exam to human judgment. Each dimension has an LLM agent that proposes improvements. A leader agent coordinates the proposals, and a Nash bargaining rule selects updates that balance progress across dimensions. Humans design the exam, review candidate changes and revise the curriculum between stages. Starting from Qwen3-VL-8B, EVA-RSI improves motion evaluation, with the largest gain on smoothness, and the gains carry over to defect types never seen during the run. On the dynamics subsets of public benchmarks, our evaluator achieves the highest observed scores among 21 tested models. As an RL reward, it increases generated motion and earns human preference. A data-selection pipeline incorporating it also increases motion.
title: EVA-RSI: Recursive Self-Improvement of Video Evaluators for Judging Temporal Quality

abstract: To advance the development of embodied general navigation, zero-shot open-vocabulary multi-object navigation has attracted increasing attention, aiming to enable robots to efficiently search multiple objects in unseen environments without training. For this task, the key lies in improving navigation policies from earlier searches to locate subsequent goals more efficiently. Recent methods automate this process through trajectory reflection and rule revision, enabling policy self-improvement. However, the mechanisms for diagnosing problems and generating revisions are typically designed by humans and remain fixed across iterations. Consequently, the system's capacity for continued self-improvement remains constrained, even as its navigation policy evolves. To this end, we propose RPSI-Nav, a Recursive Policy Self-Improvement framework for zero-shot multi-object navigation that revises both the navigation program and its revision mechanism. RPSI-Nav diagnoses search behavior, requests diagnostic views when existing observations cannot distinguish competing causes, and generates targeted navigation revisions. Feedback from subsequent goal searches is linked to the rules that produced these revisions, guiding changes to diagnosis, observation acquisition, and revision planning. The updated improver governs subsequent navigation improvements, forming a recursive loop in which RPSI-Nav revises its own improvement process. Across goals, the robot conditionally inherits accepted program updates and spatial memory, enabling search experience to improve both future navigation and adaptation. Benchmark experiments and qualitative real-robot evaluations validate RPSI-Nav's effectiveness.
title: Improve How You Improve: Recursive Policy Self-Improvement for Zero-Shot Open-Vocabulary Multi-Object Navigation

abstract: The growing volume of topically similar papers makes it difficult to identify new work that can offer useful research insights or methodological guidance. We present KnowMe Paper Radar, a lightweight discovery tool that combines multiple sources of evidence into personalized reading priorities. Users specify topics, priorities, exclusions and dates; the system brings together topical relevance, recency, author research histories, collaboration paths and direction-specific institutional context. By exposing each score component and its supporting sources, KnowMe helps readers select promising papers for their current questions and discover relevant work beyond familiar authors. Automatic acquisition, version merging and graph-cache reuse keep this workflow convenient without large language model (LLM) inference during ordinary use. Experiments on 174,640 acquired records show more than threefold faster repeated context preparation, while cached abstracts improve normalized discounted cumulative gain at rank 10 (NDCG@10) from 0.412 to 0.598 on expert-judged retrieval tasks. Complementary analyses examine how the same accumulated records support semantic retrieval, research-history modeling and literature-grounded planning. A browser interface and a structured command-line interface (CLI) make these capabilities available to both researchers and research agents, positioning KnowMe as a practical upstream tool for literature-informed recursive self-improvement (RSI) workflows.
title: KnowMe Paper Radar: Lightweight Discovery of Promising Papers in the Age of Autoresearch

abstract: Large-scale, multi-agent self-play trains robust driving policies effectively in simulation, but controlling these models to generate specific, safety-critical edge cases remains a key challenge. Existing goal-conditioned self-play frameworks rely primarily on static map-location goals and fail to reliably produce complex agent interactions such as aggressive tailgating or adversarial cut-offs. These agent interactions are necessary for rigorous autonomous vehicle (AV) testing. To address this, we present an extended multi-agent self-play framework that introduces agent-relative dynamic goals. By conditioning policies on this extended goal representation, our framework enables targeted, controllable scenario synthesis. We demonstrate that our approach successfully generates interactive driving behaviors that static-goal baselines cannot simulate, providing a flexible tool for long-tail scenario generation in AV testing.
title: Learning to Interact in Multi-Agent Self-Play for Controllable Autonomous Driving Scenario Generation

abstract: Human vision and video stereo networks both reuse disparity evidence across time, yet a refresh of the input can invalidate a match formed milliseconds earlier. What tells a system whether an old match still counts? We answer this from limited human data in three steps. First, nine temporal mechanisms share a frozen binocular-energy front end and an equal-capacity readout, so held-out behavior isolates the temporal selection rule: on 240 conditions from 10 observers, down-weighting aged evidence that has lost binocular support lowers subject RMSE from 12.6% to 10.3% and reproduces a period-dependent reversed-depth illusion, across all 59 readings of the unpublished protocol and 8 front-end perturbations. Second, four propositions establish what such data can identify: gating is identified at the level of the refresh schedule, and candidate binding is invisible to standard stimuli but exposed by a single-eye geometry flip that separates the readouts by up to 7.1%. Third, the identified rule becomes a two-field stereo memory that separates sample validity from hypothesis support. It removes a 50 ms recovery lag after geometry flips, and its regime analysis explains why plain integration stays preferable on MPI-Sintel, where 71.1% of pixels change appearance but not disparity.
title: Old Matches, New Frames: Schedule-Gated Stereo Memory from Human Vision to Machine Matching

abstract: We introduce Clover-35B-A3B-Preview (Clover), a mixture-of-experts diffusion language model with 35 billion total parameters and 3 billion activated parameters, supporting thinking-mode generation. Clover adapts Gated Delta Networks to block diffusion by combining recurrent memory of previously generated context with bidirectional softmax attention inside the current block. Historical memory readout competes with current-block tokens in a shared softmax, with learnable block-size calibration and a separate, zero-initialized right-context convolution branch. Clover leads the seven evaluated agent metrics, including 73.6 on SWE-bench Verified and 51.7 on Terminal-Bench 2.1. On internal agent workloads, it reaches a reported generation speed of 680 tokens/s using one NVIDIA GB300 GPU at BF16 precision and batch size one. We organize the evaluation around model quality, drafting and verification costs, and deployment under constrained memory. We also describe a decision-model variant that generates answers to related questions in one denoising pass. On an internal set of 500 groups, joint prediction raises question accuracy from 90.37% to 93.88% and all-correct group accuracy from 65.4% to 77.0%.
title: Clover-35B-A3B-Preview Technical Report

abstract: Building a small language model requires choosing which published improvements to combine. We compare five changes in the same model, using the same data and training budget. We test selected combinations and repeat each one with a second random seed. Mixture-of-experts layers, Muon optimisation and a Gated DeltaNet hybrid give the largest gains. Extra normalisation also helps, while an attention gate with a matched parameter budget adds little on average. The gains mostly combine, but small interactions between changes appear again in the repeated runs. Repetition also reveals benefits that an initial statistical estimate treated as noise. These findings apply to our small-model training setting; the expert models also have greater total capacity. The practical lesson is to test promising components together and repeat the comparisons before deciding which ones to keep.
title: Do Frontier Model Ingredients Add Up? A Replicated Factorial Study of Small Language Models

abstract: GPUs are expensive, yet latency-critical large language model (LLM) inference leaves part of them idle. Colocation reclaims this capacity by running best-effort work, such as fine-tuning, alongside serving. Many leading LLMs now use a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture, which adds a new source of idle time. Under expert parallelism, MoE experts are spread across GPUs, and because the router sends uneven numbers of tokens to each GPU, lightly loaded GPUs wait for the most loaded one. Even after applying load balancing solutions, such bubbles still take 8--13% of prefill time. We present BubbleTea, the first colocation system that leverages expert-parallel bubbles for fine-tuning. Unlike existing colocation systems, which make one scheduling decision for all GPUs per forward pass, BubbleTea predicts each GPU's bubble at every layer from the router's token assignment, and fills it with short chunks of fine-tuning work that reuse the weights already loaded for serving. We also introduce compiler passes that automatically derive these chunks from the served LLM as-is, without porting each model architecture to a separate training engine. Our evaluation on three MoE models, served on four A100 GPUs, shows that fine-tuning throughput with BubbleTea is 1.9--6.2$\times$ faster than with LLMStation, a state-of-the-art colocation system. BubbleTea keeps p90 inference latency within 10% of serving alone in 50 of 63 workloads, compared to 44 for LLMStation. On bursty production traces, BubbleTea trains 3.3$\times$ faster than LLMStation and 14$\times$ faster than a stock trainer colocated under CUDA MPS, with p90 inference latency staying within 7% of serving alone.
title: Harvesting Expert-Parallel Bubbles for Fine-Tuning

abstract: Transient noise artifacts ("glitches") in the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO), Virgo and KAGRA (LVK) detectors can mimic astrophysical signals and reduce confidence in gravitational-wave detections. The LVK's iDQ pipeline identifies these glitches by analyzing correlations between auxiliary sensors and the strain channel using the Ordered Veto List (OVL) algorithm. We revisit neural-network approaches to this problem using modern training infrastructure and introduce two architectures: GIANTS, a single network trained on all auxiliary-channel features, and TITAN, a mixture-of-experts model composed of subsystem-specific networks and a learned combiner. Evaluated on ten independent test periods spanning LIGO's third observing run, both models outperform OVL on most test sets, with TITAN providing the most consistent performance over time. We further show that nearly all predictive information contained in Omicron trigger features is captured by a simple binary indicator of auxiliary-channel activity. Networks trained on these binary inputs achieve essentially the same performance as models using the full 8,440-dimensional feature set while reducing the input dimensionality by an order of magnitude. These results demonstrate that modern neural networks provide a robust alternative to OVL and suggest that substantially simpler data representations are sufficient for accurate glitch identification in future iDQ deployments.
title: Neural-Network Identification of LIGO Noise Transients Using Binary Auxiliary-Channel Activity

abstract: Physics-informed neural network (PINN) optimization depends on global properties of the underlying PDE and how the physics residual evolves across the domain. Standard optimizers such as Adam use fixed gradient-based statistics, while learned PINN optimizers replace the fixed rule with a learned update built from local parameters and optimization-history features. However, none explicitly use PDE-level information. We study two coupled design questions: what PDE-level information should a learned optimizer observe, and how should that information influence its update? We introduce an 11-dimensional PDE state-capturing operator structure, residual geometry, and short-horizon update response, and use it to condition a structured meta-learned optimizer through bounded feature-wise modulation. Repeated design studies identify the compact residual-geometry state G2 and bounded FiLM as the strongest overall choices among those tested. The resulting PDE-State-conditioned optimizer improves all evaluation metrics (relative-L2, L1, solution MSE, and physics MSE) over Adam and the unconditioned learned optimizer on Linear Advection, KdV, and Burgers.
title: PDE-State Conditioning for Learned Optimization Using Physics-Informed Neural Networks

abstract: Let $c(n,k)$ denote the coefficient of $r^{(n-1)^2-k}$ in the Ehrhart polynomial of the $n\times n$ Birkhoff polytope. For every fixed nonnegative integer $k$, we prove that $c(n,k)/c(n,0)\sim n^{3k}/(2^k k!)$ as $n\to\infty$, confirming a conjecture of Stanley.
title: Proof of Stanley's Conjecture on the Leading Ehrhart Coefficients of the Birkhoff Polytope

abstract: Let $A$ be a symmetric matrix over $\mathbb{F}_2$ on a finite index set, and let $t$ be the column of diagonal entries of $A$, viewed over $\mathbb{R}$. A real detector of $A$ is a real matrix whose principal minors equal the integer $0/1$ representatives of the corresponding principal minors of $A$. We prove that $A$ has a real detector if and only if it has one of the form $K+tt^T$, with $K$ skew-symmetric and $\{0,\pm1\}$-valued. These conditions are equivalent to the existence of a principally unimodular skew-symmetric signing of the bordered lift matrix of $A$, and to regularity of the parity lift of its delta-matroid. If the graph on the nonempty index set of $A$, with edges given by its nonzero off-diagonal entries, is connected, every real detector of $A$ is diagonally similar to a detector of this form. The proof uses cut-transposes to preserve the prescribed symmetric part up to diagonal similarity, then applies feasible singleton pivots to a minimal counterexample. For ribbon bouquets, the characterization proves Whistler's conjecture. For every $A$ with a real detector, the feasible-set generating polynomial is Hurwitz stable, and the polynomial counting feasible sets of sizes $2i-1$ or $2i$ by $i$ has only strictly negative real zeros and ultra-log-concave coefficients.
title: Real Principal-Minor Detectors: Normal Forms and Regular Parity Lifts

abstract: For every strength, we prove the existence of rational designs on spheres, orthogonal and unitary groups, real and complex Grassmannians, and ellipsoids that are defined by positive-definite quadratic forms with rational coefficients and have a rational point. This answers Bannai's Problem for these spaces, solves the problem of Cui--Xia--Xiang on rational spherical $4$-designs on the unit circle, and proves Xiang's conjecture in the stronger form of existence in every dimension. To this end, we introduce the $(G,\mathcal{S})$-Prouhet--Tarry--Escott problem for an abelian group $G$ and a finite set of characters $\mathcal{S}$ and develop its existence and minimality theory. We also prove a general theorem transforming integer-weighted rational designs into equi-weighted designs on distinct rational points. On the unit circle $\mathbb{S}^1$, we determine the minimum sizes of rational spherical designs of strengths $4,5,6,7$ and show that they are respectively $2304,4608,9216,9216$. We also show that the minimum size of a rational spherical $5$-design on $\mathbb{S}^2$ is $192$. We further apply our framework to prove a conjecture of Thuswaldner--Ziegler on sums of distinct units and to answer Mahabaduge's problem on convex equilateral lattice polygons affirmatively.
title: Rational Designs and Prouhet--Tarry--Escott Problems

abstract: For a fixed integer $r\geqslant 3$, the random $r$-generalized triadic process starts from a minimum weakly $K_r$-saturated graph, namely the complete $(r-1)$-partite graph $K_{1^{r-2},n-r+2}$ with $r-2$ singleton parts and one part of size $n-r+2$. At each step of the process a new edge $\boldsymbol{e}$ is added with probability $p$, provided there exists a copy of $B_{r-2}$ in $K_n$ for which $\boldsymbol{e}$ is its spine and the only edge that has not yet been added to the current graph, where $B_{r-2}$ denotes a triangular book graph consisting of $r-2$ triangles sharing a single common edge known as the spine of the book. When $r=3$, this is the random triadic process. Korándi et al. proved a sharp threshold probability ${p}= \frac 12n^{ - \frac 12}$ for the propagation of the random triadic process.Tian and Yang complemented those results by considering the final size of the random $r$-generalized triadic process when ${p}=o( n^{- \frac 12}\log^{ α(3-r)} n)$ for any fixed constant $α> \frac 12$.In this note, we further consider the sharp threshold probability $\tilde{p}_r$ for the propagation of the random $r$-generalized triadic process when $r\geqslant 4$. We prove that $\frac 12 n^{- \frac 12}<\tilde{p}_r\leqslant c\, n^{- \frac 12}\log^{ \frac 12} n$ for some positive constant $c$, and conjecture that $\tilde{p}_r= c_r\, n^{ - \frac 12}$, where $c_r= \frac 12(r-2)!^{ \frac{1}{2r-4}}\bigl( \frac{2r-5}{r-2}\bigr)^{ \frac{2r-5}{2r-4}}$.
title: Note on the random triadic process II

abstract: The strong chromatic index $χ_s^{\prime}(G)$ of a graph $G$ is the minimum number of colors in an edgecoloring in which distinct edges at distance at most two in the line graph receive different colors. Let $θ(G)=\max _{x y \in E(G)}\left(d_G(x)+d_G(y)\right)$ denote the maximum edge weight, also called the Ore-degree, of $G$. We prove that every finite loopless multigraph $G$ with $θ(G) \leq 9$ satisfies $χ_s^{\prime}(G) \leq 28$. For simple graphs, this improves the direct greedy bound from 32 to 28. In particular, it verifies the Erdős-Nešetřil conjecture for simple graphs of maximum degree five whose vertices of degree five form an independent set, using one fewer color than the conjectured bound of 29. When $θ(G)=9$, our bound is four colors above the bound of 24 predicted by the Ore-degree conjecture of Chen, Huang, Yu, and Zhou.
title: Strong chromatic index of graphs with Ore-degree at most nine

abstract: Let \(1\le t\le k\le n\) and \(2k<n+t\). We prove that a largest \(t\)-intersecting family of subsets of \([n]\) of size at most \(k\) is obtained by taking all such subsets that contain at least \(t+r\) points of a fixed \((t+2r)\)-element set, for some \(0\le r\le\left\lfloor\frac{n-t}{2}\right\rfloor\). This settles a conjecture of Ahlswede, Bey, Engel and Khachatrian from 2002.
title: A complete intersection theorem for sets of bounded size

abstract: Corless studied the skew-symmetric tridiagonal matrices $T_m(u)$ with superdiagonal $u \in \{1, i\}^{m-1}$. He showed that $T_m(u)$ can be nilpotent only if $m = 2^K - 1$ and that the $2^{K-1}$ vectors $u$ obtained from the empty vector by repeated application of $u \mapsto (u, 1, i, \rev u)$ and $u \mapsto (u, i, 1, \rev u)$ give nilpotent matrices, and he conjectured that there are no others. We prove this conjecture. Reducing the characteristic polynomial modulo $4$ gives a necessary condition for nilpotency that is linear over $\F$. For $m > 1$ it forces $u = (v, 1, i, \rev v)$ or $u = (v, i, 1, \rev v)$, and an identity implicit in Corless's proof then reduces the problem to $v$. Since $T_m(u)$ is diagonally similar to a finite section of the Feinberg--Zee hopping matrix, the theorem also determines the nilpotent tridiagonal sign matrices. We further show that the $(1,1)$ entry of the resolvent of a nilpotent $T_m(u)$ is $λ^{-1} \pm λ^{-3} \pm λ^{-7} \pm \dots \pm λ^{-(2^K - 1)}$, with signs that determine $u$. The proof of the main theorem has been formalised in Lean~4.
title: Nilpotent skew-symmetric tridiagonal Bohemian matrices: a proof of Corless's conjecture

abstract: We prove that computing geodesic distance on the boundary of a rational convex $4$-polytope is NP-hard. We then construct rational $4$-polytopes with two rational points joined by exponentially many shortest paths of equal rational length, disproving several conjectures along the way. For the same problem, we also prove SQRTSUM-hardness under deterministic polynomial-time Turing reductions. By a separate argument, we show that the square of the geodesic distance between distinct rational boundary points of a rational convex polytope is a totally positive multiquadratic number.
title: Convexity is overrated: Shortest paths on 4-polytopes are hard to compute

abstract: This chapter surveys fundamental results for binary classification under label noise. Binary classification under label noise involves training models on datasets where class labels are partially incorrect, leading to degraded performance and misclassification. We distinguish poisoning attacks from noise processes and formalize random classification noise, Massart noise, and malicious classification noise within the probably approximately correct (PAC) framework. These models capture different adversarial strengths and data-generation realities. We then highlight some core ideas and representative results. In particular, we explain why random classification noise preserves the expected ordering of hypotheses and thus supports learning using the empirical risk minimization (ERM) principle, how sample complexity depends on the noise rate, and why learning algorithms often require an upper bound on the corruption level, as well as how such a bound may be estimated from data in the case of random classification noise. We also discuss computational aspects of ERM under noise and present a canonical negative result technique -- the method of induced distributions -- within the malicious noise model where the adversary has more power and may affect not only the label of an example but also the instance. We conclude with pointers to related work and a taxonomy that organizes classical label-noise models using the NCAR/NAR/NNAR lens.
title: Fundamentals for Binary Classification Under Label Noise

abstract: Partial spread ($\mathcal{PS}$) bent functions are Boolean functions of maximum nonlinearity built from families of subspaces that pairwise intersect only in the null vector. We design an Evolution Strategy (ES) to construct such partial spread families, comparing two encodings: one based on generator matrices of the subspaces, and one based on spread sets. With the latter, combined with a ruin-and-rebuild operator, the ES finds $\mathcal{PS}$ functions up to $n=10$ variables. An ablation study shows that mutation is necessary, while the population size is not, and that a restarted look-ahead greedy heuristic outperforms the ES on the hardest instance. We investigate this finding with a landscape analysis of the stagnation points, and we also introduce a quality-diversity variant of the ES which finds $\mathcal{PS}$ functions of low algebraic degree for 8 variables. Interestingly, the bent functions evolved by the ES have higher 2-ranks and mostly higher degrees than those obtained by a baseline Genetic Programming optimizer.
title: A Matter of Representation: Evolving Partial Spreads for Bent Functions

abstract: We formulate undersampling mask design for Cartesian magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) as a feature subset selection problem. Each sampling line is represented by a binary feature indicating whether it is included in each candidate mask. Using candidate masks and their training-set evaluations, we estimate mutual information (MI) and conditional mutual information (CMI). These estimates and a sampling-count penalty define a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) model. The model is solved using simulated annealing and quantum annealing to determine a feature subset and its corresponding sampling mask. We assess the selected subsets on the test set through zero-filled reconstruction in Fourier undersampling simulations using fastMRI knee magnitude reference images, with patient-disjoint training and test sets. At all six tested target sampling rates from 15% to 40%, the resulting reconstructions have lower mean root mean square error than those obtained with four conventional sampling methods. They also have higher mean structural similarity than those obtained using univariate mutual-information ranking at all tested rates. These results support information-theoretic feature selection as an approach to MRI undersampling mask design under the tested zero-filled simulation settings.
title: QUBO-based feature selection for MRI undersampling pattern design

abstract: We study the problem of computational efficiency for linear bandits in high-dimensional settings with a finite arm set. In linear bandits, the increase in the dimension $d$ of the feature vectors leads to growing computational costs of $O(d^2)$ at each round of update. Traditional low-rank approximation methods such as SOFUL reduce computation via fixed-size matrix sketching, yet run the risk of incurring vacuous linear regret when the spectral tail of the data is heavy and the approximation rank is inadequately selected. To guarantee regret convergence and effectively reduce computational costs, we introduce a clustering mechanism and propose the Coordinate Basis Linear Bandit (CBL) algorithm. Our method preserves the full covariance information in each cluster by maintaining an exact orthonormal basis of the cluster's column space together with a low-dimensional coordinate representation, which guarantees robust sublinear regret without spectral-tail vulnerabilities. It performs cluster switching by assigning a sentinel for each cluster, and reduces per-round update computation to $O(\bar r^2)$ in the cluster's effective dimension $\bar r=\min(r,l)$, where $r$ is the intrinsic rank of the data and $l<d$ is a tunable rank bound.
title: Coordinate Basis Linear Bandits with Sublinear Regret over Low-Rank Clusters

abstract: We study the stochastic multi-armed bandit problem in which the reward associated with each arm is the survival probability at a pre-specified time horizon, and the observed outcome is a right-censored time-to-event variable. Standard bandit algorithms face delayed and partial observations in this setting. Prior adaptations for the Kaplan--Meier (KM) estimator rely on Hoeffding-type bounds that ignore the inherent heteroscedasticity of continuous survival processes. To bridge this gap, we propose KM-UCB, a variance-adaptive policy that unites continuous-time survival analysis with discrete sequential decision-making. By leveraging martingale theory and continuous influence functions, we derive a fixed-cohort empirical Bernstein bound parameterized by Greenwood's variance formula. For realtime allocation, we retain the Greenwood index and use a survival bound from completed records to review the recommended arm. Under catch-up reporting, the policy has logarithmic expected regret with an arm-specific variance term in the exploration bound. We evaluate the original policy in a dual-layer delayed simulation and a retrospective replay of breast cancer trial data, and evaluate the correction in a separate paired simulation.
title: Variance-Adaptive Upper Confidence Bounds for Multi-Armed Bandits with Kaplan--Meier Survival Estimation

abstract: Long-term memory is essential for personalized agentic systems that interact with users over long time periods, yet current architectures only capture what happened while leaving the reasoning of why it happened to be derived later by underlying LLMs.%, and silo knowledge within individual users. These events can, however, convey not only what a user experienced but also how that experience shaped their behavioral patterns. We introduce STARK, a dual-graph memory architecture which treats these events not just as nodes but also as edges between behavioral insights. STARK maintains an Episodic Graph which records interactions as temporally, causally, and semantically linked episodes; and an Insight Graph which represents LLM-extracted behavioral signals scored by how many events support them, connected by the very events that led to them. At inference, behavioral knowledge is retrieved directly from insight nodes grounded by event-as-edges, eliminating repeated episodic traversal. The event-as-edge structure also naturally enables projecting the knowledge graph into a relational embedding space where cross-user transfer becomes possible under shared contextual circumstances, allowing the system to infer missing insights for cold-start users. Evaluations show that STARK improves by 1.48 judge score on LongMemEval information extraction and 0.93 on LoCoMo open domain questions over state of the art. On the public LongLaMP abstract-generation benchmark, cross-user transfer improves open-ended judge scores by 0.7 points and ROUGE-L by 3 at 5% graph sparsity.
title: STARK: Moving towards Personalized Agents That Truly Learn and Remember

abstract: Objective: Case investigation and contact tracing are labor-intensive. Web forms struggle when respondents need clarification before disclosing contacts, and open-ended chatbots may deviate from protocols. We developed and evaluated Epira, a protocol-controlled large language model (LLM) interviewer for multi-disease case investigation and contact tracing. Materials and Methods: Epira pairs LLM dialogue with a rule-based controller enforcing required questions, safety handoffs, and a structured case record, and adapts to new diseases by questionnaire upload. Local (Qwen2.5) and cloud (GPT-5.4) backends were tested. Study 1 used 108 simulated cases with ground-truth fields and contacts for measles and gonorrhea under Epira and open-ended conditions (864 sessions). Study 2 enrolled 72 volunteers in a 2$\times$2 disease-by-model interview assessing completion, usability, acceptability, and trust. Results: Across Study 1, Epira with a local LLM captured 88.9% of required fields and 60.1% of ground-truth contacts. Open-ended interviewers recovered 31.1-41.9 percentage points fewer required fields than the same models in Epira. In Study 2, completion was 100%; mean adapted System Usability Scale (SUS) was 82.95 $\pm$ 16.17 on a 0-100 scale and mean trust was 3.85 $\pm$ 0.77 on a 1-5 scale. Discussion: Protocol control drove completeness more than model choice. Local and cloud deployments produced similar records, supporting privacy-preserving local use with human review of routed interviews and missed contacts. Conclusion: Epira recovers required fields and contacts under diverse disclosure conditions, works with local and cloud LLMs, and received favorable usability and trust ratings.
title: Design and Evaluation of Epira: An Automated Interview System for Case Investigation and Contact Tracing

abstract: Task-specific rubrics are increasingly used to evaluate open-ended language-model outputs, yet constructing comprehensive evaluation criteria from complex source documents remains challenging. We study automatic rubric construction in professional mergers and acquisitions (M&A) due diligence, where evaluation criteria must be inferred from task instructions and supporting documents without access to an expert-authored reference rubric. We introduce a multi-axis generation framework that explores complementary structural and free-form views of the source evidence to construct a broad pool of candidate evaluation criteria. To distinguish failures of criterion discovery from failures of candidate selection, we introduce the coverage-selection gap, which measures the difference between reference-free ranking and a reference-informed greedy diagnostic under a fixed selection budget. Developed on 16 tasks and evaluated on four held-out tasks, our framework achieves 0.876 macro recall against senior-authored reference rubrics under an LLM-based criterion-equivalence protocol. Ablation studies further show that introducing new structural search axes improves recall by 6-10 percentage points, whereas increasing generation volume along existing search directions yields at most 1.5 points. These findings suggest that, once a high-coverage candidate pool has been constructed, effective reference-free selection becomes a substantial bottleneck in document-grounded rubric construction.
title: The Coverage Selection Gap: Ranking, Not Generation, Limits LLM Rubric Construction

abstract: Time series foundation models as well as the language-guided analytical agents achieve strong accuracy on standard chronological benchmarks. However, models that rank highest on historical validation splits often degrade across non-stationary regime transitions. We hypothesise that this gap arises from using historical backtesting as an open-ended search and model-selection objective instead of using it to test pre-specified compositional assumptions. Real-world time series are generated by recurring latent primitives that co-move within finite historical windows. Under strong historical co-movement, chronological holdout error cannot separate predictors that learn invariant couplings among primitives from predictors that fit transient historical correlations. Searching over large pools of architectures, hyperparameters, or chain-of-thought rules further biases selection toward historical shortcuts. Through theoretical analysis and diagnostic experiments on a controlled multi-primitive benchmark and German day-ahead electricity prices, we show that expanding validation search fails to improve out-of-regime accuracy, and that decomposing primitives without an ex-ante falsification test still breaks down when residual correlations shift. Hence, we propose formulating time series forecasting and reasoning around falsifiable compositional hypotheses that combine neural primitive encoders, explicit coupling constraints, and training-calibrated falsification tests.
title: Falsifiable Compositional Reasoning in Time Series Forecasting

abstract: Looped vision-language models (VLMs) deepen visual reasoning by repeatedly applying weight-tied modules. However, their decoding memory grows with recurrent depth and limits the image size and batch size that fit in a fixed memory budget. Each recurrent step produces its own key-value (KV) states, so the cache holds several copies of the same image. We find that, after an exact prefill, earlier steps still need access to visual information but can reuse the final visual KV within the same module. We propose FoldCache, which compresses visual KV along the recurrent axis while preserving the full prefill computation. FoldCache partitions recurrent steps within each module into groups and retains the final visual KV of each group for its members to share during decoding. Sharing stays within module boundaries, while question and answer KV remain separate for each step. The grouping granularity controls the degree of compression, and folding can be combined with token eviction and quantization to further reduce memory use. On LoopVL, FoldCache approximately halves prefix KV memory while matching full-cache accuracy on five open-ended benchmarks. These memory savings support batch sizes up to 1.7 times those of a full cache under the same GPU memory budget, and up to 2.6 times with the more aggressive FoldCache-Lite.
title: Fold the Loop: Decoding-Time KV Memory for Looped Vision-Language Models

abstract: General-purpose artificial intelligence (AI) assistants are increasingly embedded in everyday life, transforming how people accomplish tasks and potentially reshaping how they interact with others. Prior research has focused on how using AI for explicitly social purposes affects users' psychological well-being and social lives. Yet such uses account for only a small portion of interactions with general-purpose AI assistants. Whether using AI for everyday, instrumental tasks affects users' psychological well-being and social behavior remains unclear. Here we investigate these effects through a longitudinal deactivation experiment with active ChatGPT users (N=625), in which participants were randomly assigned to abstain from using AI assistants for either fourteen days (treatment) or one day (control). Participants used AI predominantly for instrumental purposes, with 84.7% reporting productivity as their most frequent use case. Two weeks of deactivation significantly reduced loneliness relative to the control group ($β= -0.10$, $p=0.03$), with reductions persisting two weeks after participants resumed using AI ($β= -0.16$, $p=0.02$). Deactivation also significantly increased the number of people participants interacted with in person and the time they spent socializing over the intervention period. Open-ended responses indicate that during the deactivation period participants sought help from others for tasks they otherwise would have delegated to AI and redirected attention toward social interaction. Overall, our findings suggest that even when AI is used primarily to accomplish instrumental tasks, it may inadvertently reduce opportunities for social interaction and connection.
title: AI Deactivation Reduces Loneliness and Increases Social Interaction

abstract: In recent years, multi-display signage (MDS) has become increasingly common in urban stations, plazas, and other public spaces, where it is primarily used to present advertisements and information. Beyond these conventional applications, MDS offers opportunities to shape people's experiences of public environments through spatially distributed and dynamic visual content. Motivated by the potential of mediated nature to support restorative experiences in urban environments, we conducted a nine-day exploratory field study in a free-admission area of a science museum, presenting artificial intelligence (AI)-generated nature videos across four displays and collecting 1,263 questionnaire responses. We combined three complementary analyses. First, structural equation modeling identified strong associations among perceived consistency across displays, presence, and self-reported restorative responses, consistent with our theoretically motivated model. Second, exploratory comparisons across video-presentation configurations revealed modest differences in consistency and restoration ratings, although these AI-generated videos did not significantly outperform the advertisement reference. Third, qualitative analysis of open-ended responses identified fascination, immersion, and restorative feelings, alongside concerns about naturalness, visual quality, and motion-related discomfort. Together, these findings provide empirical insights into MDS-mediated nature experiences, with implications for nature-video design and questionnaire refinement. They also inform a tentative conceptual extension of the model incorporating additional perceptual and evaluative factors.
title: Towards Restorative Urban Spaces: An Exploratory Field Study of Nature Videos on Public Multi-Display Signage

abstract: It is a classical result that the definable isomorphisms of the simply typed lambda-calculus with function types are exactly the hereditary permutations, and that they are generated by $A \to B \to C \cong B \to A \to C$ and congruence. We give a new proof of this result that stays inside beta-normal eta-long typed terms and uses no completeness theorem: an induction that descends through both components of an isomorphism at once. We then go one level up and prove a coherence theorem: two derivations of an isomorphism denote the same isomorphism if and only if they are equal modulo an explicit list of equations (groupoid laws, functoriality, involution, naturality and the braid equation), so these equations present the groupoid of isomorphisms, a hereditary version of the Coxeter presentation of the symmetric groups. All results are formalised in Agda, on intrinsically typed syntax with hereditary substitution, without postulates. The work is a case study for the syntactic completeness conjecture of University Algebra, a proposed solution of Tarski's high school algebra problem using dependent types, whose semantic counterpart is open. We explain the motivation and which parts of the method we expect to carry over.
title: Hereditary permutations for simple types revisited: A baby case for University Algebra

abstract: Motivated by the non-standard interpretations of if-then-else in probabilistic and quantum programs we review the different semantics of conditional branching and propose a unifying categorical structure for the interpretation of if-then-else. We show that many semantically important categories possess this structure, covering inter alia classical, probabilistic, quantum or non-deterministic computations. We examine algebraic structures related to and generated by this categorical structure, in particular on collections of predicates. In this setting we show that the skew-associativity rules of GKATs and barycentric algebras are two instances of a common skew-associativity rule.
title: On the semantics of conditional branching

abstract: We present an updated version of fosf, a reasoner for fuzzy order-sorted feature (OSF) logic, with support for flexible SPARQL query answering over RDF knowledge graphs. Fuzzy OSF logic is a knowledge representation and reasoning language where feature symbols denote functions and sort symbols denote fuzzy sets. Sorts are organized in a fuzzy subsumption relation that extends to OSF terms, record-like structures representing classes of entities. The unification algorithm for these structures provides a calculus of fuzzy type subsumption. The latest release of fosf introduces support for similarity-based reasoning by extending the OSF language with a similarity relation among sorts, alongside a translation engine for compiling OSF terms into standard SPARQL. Queries expressed as OSF terms undergo fuzzy ontology-aware rewriting prior to translation. This process incorporates an OSF theory of sort definitions, feature domain and range declarations, and fuzzy subsumption and similarity relations through fuzzy OSF constraint normalization. This rewriting enables flexible query answering by returning approximate solutions, allowing queries that would otherwise be inconsistent with the underlying ontology to yield relevant results.
title: Similarity-based OSF Logic for Flexible SPARQL Query Answering

abstract: This contribution focuses on bisimulation invariance as the hallmark of modal model theory and of modal modelling. It exemplifies traditional as well as more recent ramifications \&\ extensions of classical results -- involving variant modes of bisimulation equivalence and matching modalities also beyond plain Kripke structures, and emphasising especially the technical challenges in finite model theory and other non-elementary settings. Main results to be discussed revolve about the theme of expressive completeness phenomena: beside expressive completeness under bisimulation invariance in relation to first-order background logics, in the style of van Benthem--Rosen characterisations, this also concerns maximality results under criteria form abstract model theory, in the style of Lindstroem theorems.
title: Invariance and Expressiveness: Modal Variations

abstract: In this paper, we argue that acceptance and rejection constitute two fundamental positions necessary for inferential reasoning. Our central thesis is that a proposition acquires an inferential role when it is considered from a position of acceptance or rejection, rather than purely understood as propositional content. We distinguish between understanding a proposition, entertaining it hypothetically, and employing it within an inference. Particular attention is given to hypothetical reasoning and suspended judgement, which appear to challenge the necessity of adopting either position. We maintain that these cases do not undermine our thesis, since inferential reasoning can involve provisional acceptance or rejection without requiring personal belief or permanent commitment. Accordingly, the necessity of these positions should be understood as inferential rather than psychological. By examining the relationship between propositional content, inferential positions, and rational commitment, we defend the view that acceptance and rejection provide the fundamental conditions under which propositions can function within reasoning. This establishes a philosophical foundation for understanding inference through opposed rational positions.
title: The Necessity of Acceptance & Rejection in Inferential Reasoning

abstract: This paper concerns decision problems related to finite monoids of rational matrices. We show that determining finiteness of a given finitely presented monoid is in PSPACE, improving the known $\text{co}{-}\text{NEXP}^{\text{NP}}$ bound. We also show that the membership problem for finite matrix monoids is PSPACE-complete, improving the known NEXP-upper bound. Our two complexity results are corollaries of a new polynomial bit-size bound on matrix entries in finite monoids. This is obtained by reduction to the case of matrix groups, using the structure theory of noncommutative algebras and of matrix monoids. Our techniques also give us a polynomial-time algorithm for deciding whether a monoid of rational matrices is conjugate to a monoid of integer matrices.
title: Revisiting Finiteness of Matrix Monoids

abstract: The Burnside theorem for matrix semigroups states that a finitely generated matrix semigroup is finite whenever each element has only finitely many distinct powers. We study analogous finiteness questions for quotients of matrix semigroups by congruences, which need not themselves admit faithful finite-dimensional matrix representations. We show three finiteness criteria based on uniform bounds on the quotient images of (rank-)stable subsemigroups and groups in the Zariski closure. Our proofs use exterior algebra and the Ramsey theorem to develop variations of Simon's factorisation forest to matrix semigroups modulo congruences. We also present applications of our results to border complexity. One such involves separating homogeneous algebraic branching programs of fixed width and degree from its Zariski closure.
title: Burnside Problems for Matrix Semigroup Quotients with Applications to Border Complexity

abstract: We initiate a quantitative study of interpolation in propositional modal logic. Instead of asking only whether a logic has Craig or uniform interpolation, we measure the density of formulas, or pairs of formulas, admitting interpolants. For quasi-normal modal logics, formulas of bounded modal depth over finite signatures are counted modulo logical equivalence. We show that interpolation failure is local to cells determined by the retained signature, yielding product decompositions of both uniform and Craig interpolation densities. These decompositions allow us to analyse their asymptotic behaviour as either the retained or the forgotten signature grows. When the retained signature grows, we obtain general results for all quasi-normal modal logics; when the forgotten signature grows, the behaviour is subtler, particularly when formulas are counted after existential quantification over forgotten variables. For locally tabular logics, we introduce cell incompatibility graphs and use them for a fine-grained analysis covering tabular logics, the difference logic Diff, and bounded-depth extensions of Grz.
title: The Density of Interpolants in Modal Logic: First Results

abstract: Backpropagation remains the dominant method for training deep neural networks, but its reliance on non-local computations has motivated the search for biologically plausible alternatives. Two prominent frameworks, predictive coding (PC) and deep feedback control (DFC), offer distinct approaches to local learning, yet their relationship remains unclear. Here, we show that DFC arises as a local approximation to predictive coding dynamics near fixed points, with exact equivalence in shallow linear networks and systematic deviations arising with depth, nonlinearity, and distance from equilibrium. We characterize how this approximation, which we call Approx PC, deviates from PC in its activity dynamics, and show that these deviations can be mitigated by relinearizing the feedback controller and approaching the output target through a sequence of intermediate nudges. In networks trained on MNIST and FashionMNIST, Approx PC reaches task performance comparable to PC trained with the same nudges, and weights learned with it transfer directly to PC inference. Our results unify energy-based and control-theoretic perspectives on learning and open the door to applying tools from control theory to the training of predictive coding networks.
title: A Control-Theoretic Approximation to Predictive Coding Dynamics

abstract: Neural tracking, the temporal alignment between a continuous stimulus and the elicited brain response, enables decoding of attention from electroencephalography (EEG), yet its application to naturalistic video remains largely unexplored and mainly relies on linear canonical correlation analysis (CCA). We investigate whether a temporal contrastive model, pairing pretrained VideoMAE features with a lightweight EEG encoder trained on a correlation-based InfoNCE objective, can strengthen EEG-video alignment. Benchmarked against CCA under three generalization regimes, the model outperforms CCA across subjects (leave-one-subject-out), matches it within the stimulus manifold (leave-video-segment-out), and falls behind CCA when extrapolating to entirely novel videos (leave-one-video-out). Because this advantage appears only for seen stimuli, we probe its basis: a sham control shows that a high accuracy does not certify genuine alignment, as a synthesized correspondence fit to the seen stimuli can reproduce it without genuine temporal alignment in the training pairs. This does not preclude practical use: on a downstream attention-decoding task with seen stimuli, the model remains better than CCA since the decoding only requires a strong statistical coupling, regardless of whether that coupling is physiologically meaningful. Using a group-averaged EEG reference, we further show that genuine, generalizable coupling is nonetheless learned, only buried in the noise of single-subject EEG. These results indicate that progress hinges on data scale, diversity, and single-subject denoising.
title: Temporal Contrastive Alignment of EEG and Naturalistic Video Only Beats Linear Decoding On In-Sample Stimuli

abstract: Networks pass signals through many layers of interconnected units, so explaining what they compute means tracing how information travels from input to output and how pathways interact. Most existing approaches analyze only pairwise interactions between components such as units, layers or attention heads. Even when these measurements are combined post hoc into a circuit, they do not capture higher-order interactions along full causal chains (paths) from input to output, and so cannot address how exponentially many paths interact to construct network computation. This leaves a large set of mechanistic questions unanswerable, for example whether inhibitory pathways veto excitatory ones, and how the two combine to yield network decisions. To address this gap, we introduce Complete Path Contribution, a method to decompose the network output into mathematically complete contributions of individual paths to study path-level interactions directly and at scale. Partial summation then induces definitions of contributions for any circuit at any granularity level, with completeness guaranteed at every level. We further present an efficient algorithm that identifies the $k$ strongest paths without examining all of them, with runtime empirically linear in $k$ rather than exponential in depth. By applying Path Contribution to benchmark image classification networks, we quantify excitatory-inhibitory interactions and show how they collectively construct network decisions at a level of detail previously unmeasurable. Furthermore, in an interpretable model of the mouse retina, it reveals how dynamic receptive fields emerge from excitatory-inhibitory interaction motifs among pathways between different cell types in response to time-varying natural stimuli. Overall, Path Contribution reveals how a network's causal pathways interact at scale to transform input to output.
title: Revealing Pathway Interactions in Network Computations with Complete Path Contribution

abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) integrate visual and textual information, but their outputs do not reveal internal concept representations. Global workspace theory (GWT) proposes that information is selected from parallel brain processes, integrated in a shared workspace, and made available to specialised processes. We introduce the Multimodal Concept Lens (MC-Lens), a multimodal Jacobian lens, to study these functions in VLM concept processing. Its vision encoder and language decoder lenses map intermediate states to a shared semantic space defined by the decoder's output vocabulary to compare concept accessibility across modalities. MC-Lens supports internal concept interventions to examine the role of accessed concepts in downstream computation. (i) Accessibility and selective access. Multimodal concept information is readable in intermediate states and selectively accessible as tasks require. We extend "readout carriers" from one name token to a token set to better capture and express concept information and support counterfactual experiments. (ii) Concepts in downstream computation. Counterfactual experiments show that accessed concept information participates in downstream computation and reasoning. (iii) Development of cross-modal alignment and selective access. We develop two J-space metrics tracking the development of cross-modal concept alignment more clearly than hidden state cosine in controlled VLM training. The experiment also shows that reliable selective access develops later than concept accessibility. (iv) Shared functions across models. Across VLM families and sizes, we find shared patterns of concept accessibility, query-dependent selectivity and cross-task intervention effects despite differences in internal organisation. These findings offer an experimental basis to study GWT in multimodal artificial systems and how it can guide cross-modal alignment improvements.
title: Probing the "Conscious" Mind: Selective Access and Global Workspace in Vision-Language Models

abstract: Global Workspace Theory (GWT), a leading theory of consciousness, holds that information becomes conscious when it is broadcast to specialized processes that use it. Building a workspace into a network does not reveal what the trained network computes with it: a module that reports an answer may have combined a broadcast message with its own knowledge, or merely forwarded an answer computed elsewhere, and task accuracy and ablation cannot tell these apart. We introduce a causal protocol that identifies who computes when modules communicate. Its central test transplants a message from another input, chosen so that ignoring, relaying and recombining it predict three different answers. On networks built to relay or to recombine, the test assigns the right computation in every case. Among trained workspace models it finds all three outcomes: one leaves its broadcast nearly unused, and of two models that differ only in their training data, one relays and the other recombines. In AFGW, a language model whose modules communicate only through a learned workspace, a transplanted message yields the answer that recombination predicts in 97% of cases, and its content acts by redirecting what the receiver retrieves from its own memory. The tests carry over to other communication designs and to a known interface of a pretrained Transformer, turning GWT's central claim into a testable property of trained models.
title: Does the Workspace Do the Work? A Causal Protocol for Verifying Global-Workspace Computation in a Language Model

abstract: The completely packed $O(1)$ loop model can be viewed as an interface representation of critical bond percolation on the square lattice. We consider submatching events, which prescribe how these interfaces pair finitely many consecutive boundary points. Romik's rationality conjectures predict that the probabilities of these events on the semi-infinite cylinder are given by specific rational functions, which even become dyadic rationals in the half-plane limit. We derive explicit Pfaffian formulae for the probability of $k$ nested arches on the semi-infinite cylinder of circumference $2N$, valid for $k<N$. We deduce that these probabilities are rational functions of $N$ and, by taking the limit $N\to\infty$, that the corresponding half-plane probabilities remain rational. This establishes key aspects of Romik's conjectures. Our proof uses identities of Fonseca and Zinn-Justin, derived through the qKZ formalism, which express these probabilities as ratios of enumeration numbers for totally symmetric self-complementary plane partitions (TSSCPPs). These plane partitions admit a dimer representation, allowing us to apply Kasteleyn theory. We evaluate the resulting hypergeometric sum using Zeilberger's and Gosper's algorithms and then take the half-plane limit $N\to\infty$. Along the way, we derive a somewhat simplified expression for the inverse Kasteleyn matrix entries (encoding correlations in TSSCPPs) of Ayyer and Chhita, which might be of independent interest.
title: On Romik's rationality conjectures for critical percolation

abstract: Two subsets $A,B$ of a finite set $X$ are crossing if $A\cap B$, $A\setminus B$, $B\setminus A$, and $X\setminus(A\cup B)$ are all nonempty. A family is $k$-cross-free if it contains no $k$ pairwise crossing members. We construct such families on $n$ elements of size $(\frac{1}{3}+o(1))kn\log k$, where the asymptotic is taken as $k$ tends to infinity and is uniform over all integers $n\ge k$. This disproves the uniform $O(kn)$ bound conjectured by Karzanov and Lomonosov. Our construction consists of cyclic intervals with at most one point deleted, together with their complements. We also prove an $O(kn\log k)$ upper bound for $k$-cross-free families closed under all cyclic shifts of a fixed cyclic ordering of the ground set.
title: Large $k$-cross-free families

abstract: A seminal result of Hajnal and Szemerédi from 1970 asserts that every graph on $n$ vertices with $q\;|\;n$ and minimum degree at least $\Big(1-\frac{1}{q}\Big)n$ admits a $K_q$-factor (a collection of vertex-disjoint copies of $K_q$ spanning all vertices). There has been sustained interest in extending this result to hypergraph $K_q^r$-factors. For general $q$ and $r$, Lu and Székely in 2007 showed that every large enough, $r$-graph $G$ with $q\mid v(G)$ and $δ_{r-1}(G) \ge \left(1- \frac{c}{q^{r-1}}\right)v(G)$ admits a $K_q^r$-factor (where $c$ is a constant depending on $r$ but not $q$), and there have been various subsequent improvements to the constant (but not the order) of this bound over the ensuing decades. Meanwhile, results from codegree Turán theory show that $δ_{r-1}(G) \ge \left(1 - \frac{c \cdot \log q}{q^{r-1}} \right)v(G)$ is necessary. Surprisingly, our main result shows that the order of this upper bound is not correct and, in fact, the codegree $K_q^r$-factor threshold is much closer to this codegree Turán theory bound. In particular, we show that $δ_{r-1}(G) \ge \left( 1-c\cdot \frac{\log^{1-1/(r-1)}q}{q^{r-1}}\right)v(G)$ suffices for the existence of a $K_q^r$-factor. Our key contribution is showing the same is true for the fractional threshold. Inspired by the first and fourth author's recent proof of the Nash-Williams' Conjecture, we accomplish this by combining a linear programming framework with ideas from discharging. Additionally, we establish a technical result about finding large independent sets in sparse, non-uniform hypergraphs, which may be of independent interest.
title: Hypergraph Hajnal-Szemerédi

abstract: We prove that every nonconstant symmetric Boolean function on $n$ variables has exact real polynomial degree at least $n-O(n^{1/3}(\log n)^{2/3})$. This makes progress toward the conjecture of von zur Gathen and Roche that the degree is always at least $n-3$. The original prime-gap argument of von zur Gathen and Roche yields a degree deficit of $O(n^{0.525})$ using the theorem of Baker, Harman, and Pintz, or $O(n^{0.52})$ using an estimate claimed in a recent preprint. Our $\widetilde{O}(n^{1/3})$ bound on the degree deficit improves upon the $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{n})$ bound obtainable from the prime-gap approach, even assuming the Riemann hypothesis or Legendre's conjecture. Notably, our proof avoids prime-gap estimates entirely. The proof combines vanishing binomial moments with the arithmetic of linear recurrences. A quantitative form of the integer Hankel determinant method in the Pólya--Carlson theorem forces the function's values on a central interval of Hamming weights to satisfy a short rational recurrence. A second determinant argument bounds the number of characteristic roots near $-1$. Through the binomial transform, these roots can then be cancelled by a polynomial test of degree below the deficit. An integer annihilator and contour estimates make the test isolate the first failure of the recurrence, yielding a contradiction with the vanishing-moment conditions. If the recurrence agrees with the function on a sufficiently long interval, arithmetic height bounds instead force a bounded period, which is ruled out by a separate polynomial test. Every numbered result in the paper has been formally verified in Lean~4.
title: Degree Lower Bounds for Symmetric Boolean Functions: Breaking the Prime-Gap Barrier

abstract: Goulden and Jackson defined a Jack deformation $a_{μν}^λ(α)$ of the connection coefficients of the symmetric group and conjectured that these were polynomials in $b=α-1$ with nonnegative interger coefficients. This conjecture was extended to the structure constants of (stable) Jack characters by Śniady. We formulate a stronger operator conjecture: the differential operators $Δ_μ(α)$ that multiply by stable Jack characters should have coefficients in ${\mathbb N}[b]$ in the normally ordered Heisenberg basis $p_ID_J$. We provide numerical evidence, as well as theoretical consequences of the conjecture which can be rigorously proved. Namely, we exhibit two families of $α$-shifted symmetric functions whose associated differential operators are ${\mathbb N}[b]$ positive simultaneously on the bases $p_ID_J$ and $Δ_μ(α)$. These operators correspond to the Boolean cumulants of the Jack transition measure and to the Cartan generators of the affine Yangian $Y(\widehat{\mathfrak gl}_1)$.
title: An operator $b$-positivity conjecture for Jack characters

abstract: The study of dense induced bipartite subgraphs dates back to the work of Erdős, Faudree, Pach, and Spencer on triangle-free graphs. In this paper, we study this problem under different local sparsity conditions. First, we prove that for every fixed integer $t\ge 2$ and all sufficiently large $d$, every $K_{t,t}$-free graph of minimum degree at least $d$ contains an induced bipartite subgraph of average degree at least $\log d-16t\log\log d$. This follows from our bound $χ_f(G)\le d/(\log d-16t\log\log d)$ for every $d$-degenerate $K_{t,t}$-free graph $G$, which answers a problem of Allen, Dhawan, and Noel. For triangle-free $d$-degenerate graphs $G$, we prove that $χ_f(G)\le(2.85+o(1))d/\log d$, improving the leading constant 4 in the bound of Martinsson and Steiner. So every triangle-free graph of minimum degree at least $d$ contains an induced bipartite subgraph of average degree at least $(20/57-o(1))\log d$. We also extend the study of a conjecture of Esperet, Kang, and Thomassé to graphs containing triangles. We prove that if $G$ has minimum degree at least $d$ and each edge belongs to at most $d/k^2$ triangles, where $k=\lfloor\log d/\log\log d\rfloor$, then $G$ contains an induced bipartite subgraph of average degree $Ω(\log d/\log\log d)$.
title: Dense induced bipartite subgraphs under local sparsity

abstract: An $[r,n,1]$-graph has $r$ independent parts of size $n$, with a matching between each pair of parts. Yuster conjectured in 2021 that every such graph has a partition into independent transversals whenever $n\ge 2\lceil r/2\rceil$. We prove that there is an absolute constant $A>0$ such that, for all sufficiently large $r$, this partition exists whenever $n\ge\lceil r+A r^{20/21}\rceil$. Thus $f(r)\le r+O(r^{20/21})$, where $f(r)$ is the least $n_0$ such that every $[r,n,1]$-graph has such a partition whenever $n\ge n_0$. In particular, $f(r)/r\to1$, giving an asymptotic form of the conjecture.
title: An asymptotic bound for Yuster's independent transversal factor conjecture

abstract: For a positive integer $d$ let $c_d^{\mathrm{top}}$ (resp. $c_d^{\mathrm{aff}}$) be the maximum $c$ such that, for every continuous (resp. affine) map from the $n$-dimensional simplex $Δ^n$ to $\mathbb{R}^d$, some point of $\mathbb{R}^d$ lies in the images of at least $(c-o(1))\binom{n+1}{d+1}$ of the $d$-dimensional faces, as $n\to\infty$. We show that \[ c_d^{\mathrm{top}}=c_d^{\mathrm{aff}}=\frac{(d+1)!}{(d+1)^{d+1}}. \] The second equality confirms a conjecture of Bukh, Matoušek, and Nivasch, who established the upper bound. The proof was found by GPT-6 Astra, following the directions of the author.
title: Sharp topological overlap in every dimension

abstract: Learning and inference on time series can pose significant statistical challenges, including autocorrelated observations, distribution shift over time, and the curse of dimensionality. These challenges complicate the practical application of causal discovery algorithms, which already suffer from high computational and sample complexity in the general case. To mitigate these issues, this work introduces Iterative Temporal Parent Discovery (ITPD): a sound and complete constraint-based procedure for causal structure learning on multivariate time series with causal nonstationarity. ITPD takes a local-to-global learning approach that discovers the global graph by sequentially discovering the parent set for each variable. ITPD exploits temporal structural priors, graph partitioning, and the local Markov condition to swap higher-order conditional independence tests for lower-order alternatives. With an exact oracle, ITPD performed the least number of tests and used the smallest average conditioning set sizes relative to baselines. In benchmarking simulations, ITPD sat on the Pareto frontier with respect to F1 and wall-clock time and was faster than baselines on large graphs ($\geq$ 1000 nodes). For graphs with 2000 nodes, ITPD ran $2.3\times$, $9.1\times$, and $40.9\times$ faster than iterative IAMB, DF-PC, and PCMCI, respectively.
title: Time Series Structure Learning with Local Causal Parent Discovery

abstract: Attention heads specialize into distinct functions during training, often emerging in stages together with sharp changes in model behavior. While this phenomenon has mostly been studied as a function of training time, we ask how head specialization depends on the amount of available training data. Empirically, we find that heads specialized to syntactic relations in BERT emerge as the dataset size increases. We then study this phenomenon in a solvable high-dimensional model of multi-head attention and establish that, in this model, head specialization is a genuine phase transition in sample complexity, corresponding to a non-analyticity in the test error and other observables. Depending on data structure and regularization, specialization can follow uninformative head differentiation or occur through a cascade of phase transitions that progressively recover weaker latent features, providing a statistical form of simplicity bias. Finally, we relate these statistical transitions to the stagewise emergence of specialized heads during online learning, disentangling statistical from dynamical origins of head specialization.
title: Attention Head Specialization: Phase Transitions in Sample Complexity

abstract: Neural-network quantum states (NQSs) exhibit a disparity in converging to the ground state during energy minimization: while the energy converges quadratically with the error in the variational wave function, other observables converge only linearly, which limits the accuracy of physical predictions. Here we show how to close this gap by introducing a new algorithm that improves the accuracy of NQSs. Our method, termed dynamical averaging, estimates expectation values by averaging over a state (or observable) evolved in real-time. Using insights from quantum information, we prove an up-to-quadratic suppression of error in arbitrary ground state observables, thus matching the fast convergence of the energy. Importantly, this improved accuracy requires neither further energy minimization nor increased model complexity, but rather exploits the effect of randomization on quantum states. We demonstrate dynamical averaging on non-integrable spin models, where it accelerates convergence and substantially reduces errors in observables.
title: High-Accuracy Neural-Network Quantum States via Randomized Real-Time Dynamics
